note: Voiceover per section. Every scene runs: CONTEXT sentence -> action -> result -> WHY IT MATTERS sentence, and a click only ever happens AFTER the sentence that explains it. {tokens} are filled from live data at record time; a sentence that says a number is only spoken once that number is on screen. `pace` multiplies the Kokoro speed's inverse (above 1 = slower than the configured 0.9): only the pre-action check runs at the confirmed pace; the other scenes are a little quicker to fit 4:00.

sections.title: Ananya's story (illustrative)
lines: This is Ananya. Her college is holding back her certificates.
She complains to the Grievance Cell.
The Regulation Bureau already has a case on the same college.
Neither can see the other's file, so the college may be asked twice.

sections.title: Without / With Samanvay
lines: Two inboxes hold cases about the same college. Now we turn Samanvay on.
It joins {ww.pairs} pairs. {ww.noid} have no AICTE ID, and every name is spelt differently.
It finds the same college, however it is written.

sections.title: The pre-action check
lines: Now Ananya's case. The officer wants her certificate records from the college.
She picks the action and types her request.
Before anything is sent, Samanvay checks the other bureaus.
It stops her. This is AICTE's own alert: Potential Overlapping Cases, Coordination Required.
The Regulation Bureau asked for the same records {check.days} days ago.
Without this check, the college would get two requests.

sections.title: Coordinate instead
lines: The officer can coordinate, send anyway with a reason, or cancel.
She chooses to coordinate.
Samanvay drafts the note. She reads it, then sends it.
The college is asked once, and both bureaus know.

sections.title: At the Regulation Bureau
lines: The Regulation Bureau officer opens the inbox. The note is at the top.
Opening it shows both cases and one shared timeline.
Each bureau has its own thread. Once an officer confirms the match, the threads join.
So nobody acts blind.

sections.title: Stress test
lines: Does it work? Names are the hard part.
Here is one college, written {stress.total} different ways. We press Run to test them all.
Samanvay finds {stress.samanvay}. An exact-name search finds {stress.exact}. An ID-only search finds {stress.id}.
The {stress.misses} misses are shown, not hidden.

sections.title: Baselines and accuracy
lines: We compare it with two simpler methods, on {base.overlaps} planted overlaps.
An ID-only search finds {base.id}. An exact-name search finds {base.exact}, with {base.exact_wrong} wrong.
Samanvay finds {base.samanvay}, with {base.samanvay_wrong} wrong.
On a second dataset it was never tuned on, it again found {seed43.found} of {seed43.overlaps}.
This is synthetic data, so real results will be messier.

sections.title: How it works
lines: Four ideas.
One: an AICTE ID match, when both complaints have one.
Two: fuzzy name and address matching, which handles initials and abbreviations.
Three: description similarity, to spot the same issue.
Four: rule-based clash checks, before an action goes out.
The rules are explainable: no black-box AI, and a person decides.

sections.title: Reports dashboard
lines: Now, a view for senior officers.
One dashboard shows every bureau's pending, ageing and overdue cases together.

sections.title: Inbox and privacy
lines: Each officer works from one inbox.
Open another bureau's case, and the complainant's name is hidden.
Samanvay checks across bureaus at the moment an officer is about to act.
